title: Blog 1
content:
Amazon Polly Bidirectional Streaming: Accelerating Speech Synthesis for Conversational AI Applications 1. Background In conversational AI applications, users often want to hear an answer as soon as the system starts generating it, rather than waiting for the entire response to be completed. For example, a customer service chatbot may use a large language model (LLM) to generate an answer and then convert the content into speech for the user.
LLMs typically generate text incrementally during processing. However, with traditional Text-to-Speech (TTS) integration, an application generally has to provide the entire text in a single synthesis request. This means the system may need to wait until enough content is available before starting the TTS request. To reduce this delay, developers may have to split the text into multiple segments, send several synthesis requests, and handle the reassembly of the resulting audio segments.
Amazon Polly can already return audio as a stream in the response to the SynthesizeSpeech API. The limitation in this scenario is on the input side: this API requires the text to be provided in a complete request. Amazon Polly Bidirectional Streaming addresses this limitation by allowing an application to send text incrementally while receiving synthesized audio at the same time within a single connection session.
2. Introducing Amazon Polly Bidirectional Streaming Amazon Polly is an AWS-managed Text-to-Speech service that converts text into synthesized speech. It provides different voices and engines to support various text-to-audio conversion needs.
The Bidirectional Streaming feature uses the StartSpeechSynthesisStream API. This API establishes a bidirectional HTTP/2 connection between the application and Amazon Polly. Instead of waiting for the complete text, the application can send content in segments as it becomes available. At the same time, Polly synthesizes the text it has received and sends audio segments back to the application.
This mechanism has three key aspects:
Incremental text input: The application sends text segments to Polly through the TextEvent event. The text segments do not necessarily have to align with sentence or paragraph boundaries. Concurrent audio output: Polly returns audio data through the AudioEvent event as audio segments are generated. Audio events can be received while the application is still sending additional text. Controlled session closure: After all text has been sent, the application sends a CloseStreamEvent. Polly processes any remaining buffered text, sends the final audio segments, and signals completion through StreamClosedEvent. The key innovation is not that Polly supports audio streaming for the first time. Rather, it is the ability to stream both the input text and the output audio concurrently over the same HTTP/2 connection. This approach is particularly suitable for content that is generated continuously by an LLM.
3. Overall Architecture Figure 1. An illustrative architecture of a conversational AI application using Amazon Polly Bidirectional Streaming.
The illustrated architecture consists of four main components:
Component Role Web/Mobile Application Receives questions from users and plays the audio segments forwarded by the backend. Application Backend Receives requests, calls the LLM, opens a streaming session with Polly, sends text, and receives audio segments. Large Language Model (LLM) Analyzes questions and generates responses incrementally. Amazon Bedrock or another platform that supports streaming generation can be used. Amazon Polly Receives text through TextEvent, synthesizes speech using the Generative engine, and returns audio through AudioEvent. The backend coordinates communication between the LLM, Amazon Polly, and the user application. The method used to deliver audio data from the backend to a browser or mobile device is a design choice made by the developer. For example, the backend may use WebSocket or another suitable streaming mechanism. This is an application-level connection, not a requirement imposed by the HTTP/2 connection between the backend and Amazon Polly.
4. How It Works A Bidirectional Streaming session can follow this sequence:
The user submits a question: The Web or Mobile application sends the content to the backend. The backend calls the LLM: The backend forwards the question to the language model. The LLM starts generating the response incrementally instead of waiting until the entire response is complete. A session is opened with Polly: The backend calls StartSpeechSynthesisStream through a compatible AWS SDK and configures synthesis parameters such as Engine, VoiceId, OutputFormat, and SampleRate. Text is sent: Whenever a new portion of the response is received from the LLM, the backend sends that portion to Polly as a TextEvent. Audio is received: While the backend continues sending text, Polly returns audio segments through AudioEvent. The backend receives these segments and forwards them to the application. Audio is played: The application orders the audio segments and adds them to its playback buffer so that the user can listen when the data is ready. The session is closed: After the LLM has finished generating the response, the backend sends a CloseStreamEvent. Polly processes the remaining data and sends a StreamClosedEvent to indicate that the synthesis session has completed. This process allows two operations to take place in parallel: the LLM continues generating text while Polly synthesizes the text it has already received. The application does not need to wait for the LLM to finish the entire response before starting speech synthesis.
5. Comparison with the SynthesizeSpeech API To understand the value of the new feature, it is important to distinguish Bidirectional Streaming from Amazon Polly’s existing SynthesizeSpeech API.
SynthesizeSpeech follows a request–response model: the application submits the entire text in one request and then receives an audio response. The audio in that response can still be delivered progressively as it becomes available. Therefore, the main difference is not whether the older API supports audio streaming, but how the input text is provided.
By contrast, StartSpeechSynthesisStream allows the application to send text incrementally through TextEvent and receive audio through AudioEvent within the same bidirectional HTTP/2 session.
Criterion SynthesizeSpeech StartSpeechSynthesisStream How text is submitted Sends the complete text in one request Sends text incrementally through TextEvent How audio is received Receives an audio stream in the HTTP response Receives audio segments through AudioEvent Communication model Request–response Bidirectional streaming over HTTP/2 Supported engines Standard, Neural, Long-form, and Generative Generative only Speech Marks Supported Not supported Suitable use case The text is available before synthesis begins The text is generated incrementally and synthesis should begin before the LLM finishes Therefore, SynthesizeSpeech remains suitable when the application already has the complete content and needs a straightforward integration. StartSpeechSynthesisStream is more suitable when text is generated continuously, such as chatbot responses or translated content delivered in segments.
6. Performance in AWS’s Benchmark In its technical announcement, AWS conducted a benchmark using the same content of 7,045 characters, or approximately 970 words. The test used the Matthew voice with the Generative engine, MP3 output at a 24 kHz sample rate, and the US West (Oregon) Region. AWS simulated the LLM generating content at a rate of approximately 30 milliseconds per word.
Metric Sequential integration with SynthesizeSpeech Bidirectional Streaming Total processing time 115,226 ms (approximately 115 seconds) 70,071 ms (approximately 70 seconds) Number of API calls 27 1 streaming session Content submission method Sends each complete sentence sequentially Sends text incrementally as it is generated In this scenario, AWS reported an approximately 39% reduction in processing time and a decrease in API calls from 27 to 1. These results come from a specific test configuration and integration approach; they are not a guaranteed improvement for every application. Actual performance also depends on the LLM’s generation speed, network latency, voice, data segmentation, and the application’s audio playback mechanism.
7. Benefits and Use Cases Reduced perceived waiting time: Users can start listening to a response while the LLM is still generating the next portions of content. This can make voice-based conversations feel more responsive and natural.
Simplified application integration: With a traditional implementation, developers may need to split content manually, send multiple TTS requests, track the order of responses, and reassemble audio segments. Bidirectional Streaming provides a single bidirectional session, reducing some of the orchestration logic and the number of separate synthesis requests.
Support for applications that require continuous responses: The feature can be used in customer service chatbots, virtual assistants, Interactive Voice Response (IVR) systems, conversational translation applications, and accessibility tools that provide spoken content.
However, Bidirectional Streaming does not automatically eliminate all application latency. Response time is still affected by LLM processing time, network conditions, speech synthesis, and how the application delivers audio to users.
8. Limitations and Implementation Considerations Generative engine only: StartSpeechSynthesisStream currently requires the Generative engine. If an application needs the Standard, Neural, or Long-form engine, it must choose another suitable API, such as SynthesizeSpeech. Speech Marks are not supported: Applications that require Speech Marks to synchronize words, subtitles, or animations should consider an alternative approach. A compatible SDK is required: Bidirectional Streaming requires an AWS SDK that supports HTTP/2 event streams. AWS currently lists SDKs such as Java 2.x, JavaScript v3, .NET v4, C++, Go v2, Kotlin, PHP v3, Ruby v3, Rust, and Swift. According to the Developer Guide, AWS CLI, Python, and .NET v3 are not supported. For a Node.js backend, AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 can be used. Session time limits apply: A streaming session can last up to 10 minutes. If no input event is received for 5 seconds, Polly may close the session. The application needs to handle long pauses and open a new session when the content exceeds the permitted duration. Latency must be balanced against speech quality: Polly may buffer text by default so that synthesis occurs at natural language boundaries. The application can request an earlier flush, but flushing in the middle of a sentence may affect intonation or pronunciation because Polly has less context for the subsequent content. Region and voice availability must be checked: Before implementation, confirm that the Generative engine and the desired voice are available in the selected AWS Region. Do not assume that every language or Polly voice is compatible with Bidirectional Streaming. In addition, AWS credentials should be managed in the backend using an IAM Role or another appropriate access mechanism. Long-term Access Keys and Secret Access Keys should not be embedded directly in JavaScript code running in a browser or mobile application.
9. Conclusion Amazon Polly Bidirectional Streaming extends speech synthesis by allowing an application to stream input text and receive output audio concurrently over an HTTP/2 connection. This is an important improvement for conversational AI applications, where content is often generated incrementally by an LLM.
The feature can reduce users’ perceived waiting time and simplify part of the TTS integration process. However, API selection should still depend on the application’s requirements: StartSpeechSynthesisStream is suitable for continuously generated text, while SynthesizeSpeech remains a reasonable choice when the complete text is already available or when the application requires engines and features that the streaming API does not support.
References AWS Machine Learning Blog, Introducing Amazon Polly Bidirectional Streaming: Real-time speech synthesis for conversational AI, March 26, 2026. AWS What’s New, Amazon Polly expands Generative TTS engine with 10 new voices, 2 new regions, and Bidirectional Streaming API, March 20, 2026. Amazon Polly Developer Guide, Synthesizing speech with bidirectional streaming. Amazon Polly Developer Guide, SynthesizeSpeech and StartSpeechSynthesisStream compared. Amazon Polly Developer Guide, Sending text and receiving audio.

Week 1 Objectives: Get acquainted with members of First Cloud AI Journey and understand the internship program’s rules, regulations, requirements, and weekly learning roadmap. Understand the AWS Free Tier 2025 program, including its major changes, account plans, promotional credits, eligibility conditions, and account protection policies. Learn the AWS account registration process, explore the AWS Management Console, and understand how to manage account information and promotional credits. Understand AWS Budgets and its four budget types, including budget configurations, monitoring periods, usage limits, and cost alert notifications. Gain practical experience in creating and configuring AWS Budgets to monitor cloud service costs and resource usage, helping prevent unexpected AWS charges. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 2 - Get acquainted with members of First Cloud AI Journey.
- Read and understand the internship program’s rules, regulations, requirements, and working procedures.
- Review the internship learning roadmap and understand the main topics, objectives, and activities planned for each week. 05/10/2026 05/10/2026 3 - Study AWS Free Tier 2025 and understand the major changes introduced from July 15, 2025, compared to the previous Free Tier program.
- Learn about the two AWS account plans: Free Account Plan and Paid Account Plan.
- Understand the $100 initial credit granted upon registration and the additional $100 credit obtainable by completing five specified learning tasks.
- Study the benefits and limitations of the Free Account Plan, including the six-month protection period, automatic account closure conditions, and access to more than 30 Always Free services.
- Understand the Paid Account Plan, including full access to AWS services, promotional credit eligibility, short-term service trials, and charges that may apply when usage exceeds available credits.
- Compare the two account plans in terms of service access, credit usage, billing responsibilities, account protection, and account expiration. 06/10/2026 06/10/2026 AWS Free Tier 2025 4 - Study the AWS account registration process and the information required to create an AWS account.
- Learn about account setup, including email verification, account information, password configuration, account plan selection, payment method verification, and phone number verification.
- Explore the AWS Management Console and become familiar with its interface, navigation, and main service categories.
- Learn how to access the Billing and Cost Management dashboard and locate promotional credit information.
- Understand how to check credit balances, credit expiration dates, eligibility conditions, and services covered by promotional credits.
- Recognize the importance of monitoring credit usage and reviewing AWS service consumption to avoid unexpected charges. 07/10/2026 07/10/2026 AWS Free Tier 2025 5 - Study AWS Budgets and understand its role in monitoring, managing, and controlling AWS cloud service costs.
- Learn about the four main types of AWS Budgets:
+ Cost Budget
+ Usage Budget
+ Reserved Instance (RI) Budget
+ Savings Plans Budget
- Understand the differences between Cost Budget, which monitors spending, and Usage Budget, which monitors resource consumption.
- Learn how Reserved Instance Budgets monitor Reserved Instance utilization and coverage, and how Savings Plans Budgets monitor Savings Plans utilization and commitments.
- Study budget configuration options, including daily, monthly, quarterly, and annual periods.
- Understand recurring and expiring budgets, as well as fixed and planned budget amounts.
- Learn how to configure alert thresholds for actual and forecasted costs and receive email notifications when budget limits are reached or exceeded.
- Explore AWS Budget templates, particularly the Monthly Cost Budget template, and learn how to customize budget configurations according to monitoring requirements. 08/10/2026 08/10/2026 AWS Budgets - Getting Started 6 - Practice: Create and configure an AWS Budget through AWS Billing and Cost Management.
+ Access the AWS Management Console and open the Billing and Cost Management service.
+ Navigate to Budgets and select Create a budget.
+ Explore the available budget creation methods and templates.
+ Create a Monthly Cost Budget using the predefined template.
+ Specify the budget name, monthly spending limit, monitoring period, and alert thresholds.
+ Configure email notifications to receive alerts when the budget thresholds are reached or exceeded.
+ Explore customized Cost Budget settings, including budget periods, recurring or expiring budgets, and fixed or planned budget amounts.
+ Explore Usage Budget configuration and learn how to monitor EC2 running hours using the EC2: ELB - Running Hours usage type group, where available.
+ Review budget configurations, budget status, budget health, and budget history.
- Learn how to delete temporary test budgets after completing the exercises to avoid unnecessary notifications.
- Understand that deleting a budget removes its monitoring and alert configuration but does not automatically delete or stop running AWS resources. 09/10/2026 09/10/2026 AWS Budgets - Getting Started Week 1 Achievements: Became familiar with the members of First Cloud AI Journey, the internship program’s rules, regulations, requirements, and weekly learning roadmap.
Gained a comprehensive understanding of the AWS Free Tier 2025 program and its major improvements compared to the previous Free Tier model, particularly for accounts created from July 15, 2025, including:
$100 initial credit upon account registration. Additional $100 credit through five specified learning tasks, with $20 associated with each task. Two available account plans: Free Account Plan and Paid Account Plan. Six-month protection period under the Free Account Plan, subject to the program’s applicable conditions. Access to more than 30 Always Free services within their applicable free usage limits. Differences in account expiration and automatic closure between the two plans. Understood the differences between the Free Account Plan and Paid Account Plan, particularly in terms of:
AWS service availability and access restrictions. Promotional credit usage and eligibility. Billing responsibilities when usage exceeds available credits. Account protection and automatic closure conditions. Availability of additional promotional credits and short-term service trials. Gained knowledge of the AWS account registration process, including:
Providing account information and configuring account credentials. Verifying the registration email. Selecting an appropriate account plan. Providing and verifying payment information. Verifying the registered phone number. Selecting the applicable support plan. Became familiar with the AWS Management Console and learned how to navigate the interface, search for AWS services, and access the Billing and Cost Management dashboard.
Understood how to check promotional credits through the AWS Billing Console, including:
Reviewing available credit balances. Checking credit expiration dates. Understanding credit eligibility conditions. Identifying services covered by promotional credits. Monitoring credit consumption to avoid unexpected charges. Gained a comprehensive understanding of AWS Budgets and its four main budget types:
Cost Budget: Monitors actual and forecasted AWS spending against a specified budget amount and sends alerts when configured thresholds are reached or exceeded. Usage Budget: Monitors the consumption of selected AWS services against predefined usage limits, such as EC2 running hours. Reserved Instance (RI) Budget: Monitors Reserved Instance utilization and coverage to help track the usage of reserved capacity commitments. Savings Plans Budget: Monitors Savings Plans utilization and commitments to help track the usage of savings plan benefits. Understood the differences between Cost Budget and Usage Budget, particularly that Cost Budget focuses on monetary spending, whereas Usage Budget focuses on the actual consumption of AWS resources.
Gained knowledge of AWS Budget configuration options, including:
Selecting an appropriate budget type. Configuring daily, monthly, quarterly, and annual monitoring periods. Setting fixed or planned budget amounts. Configuring recurring or expiring budgets. Defining budget scopes and the AWS services to be monitored. Setting actual and forecasted cost alert thresholds. Configuring email notifications when budget thresholds are reached or exceeded. Became familiar with AWS Budget templates and learned how to use the predefined Monthly Cost Budget template to simplify budget creation and configuration.
Gained practical experience in creating and configuring an AWS Cost Budget through the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, including:
Accessing the Budgets management interface. Selecting an appropriate budget creation method. Configuring a monthly spending limit. Setting alert thresholds and email notifications. Reviewing the created budget and its configuration. Learned how to configure and monitor Usage Budgets, particularly how to select the EC2: ELB - Running Hours usage type group to monitor EC2 instance running hours.
Understood how to review budget status, budget health, and budget history to monitor spending and resource consumption over time.
Learned the importance of AWS cost management and resource cleanup, including deleting temporary test budgets after completing practical exercises to avoid unnecessary notifications.
Recognized that AWS Budget alerts are monitoring and notification mechanisms. They do not automatically stop running AWS resources or prevent additional service charges when a budget threshold is exceeded.

content:
AWS Cost Control and Optimization Strategy with Budget Controls for AWS In a cloud environment, costs do not always increase because a single service is expensive. Sometimes, many small charges from EC2 instances, EBS volumes, snapshots, or networking components accumulate over time and cause the AWS bill to exceed expectations.
One of the challenges of managing AWS infrastructure is identifying which resources still need to run, which can be stopped, and which are no longer needed. Without timely monitoring and action, these resources may continue generating costs even when they are no longer being used.
Therefore, in addition to monitoring the budget, organizations need a mechanism that connects spending thresholds with resource management rules. Budget Controls for AWS is an open-source solution that combines AWS Budgets, AWS Config, and automation services to send alerts and take actions on supported resource types.
This article focuses on how the solution works, how it can be applied as part of an AWS Cost Optimization strategy, and the considerations identified through hands-on practice with Amazon EC2.
1. OVERVIEW OF BUDGET CONTROLS FOR AWS 1.1. The Cost Control Challenge The pay-as-you-go pricing model allows users to create and scale AWS resources flexibly. However, if resources are not managed after a task is completed, they may continue to incur costs.
Common scenarios include:
An EC2 instance remains running even though it is no longer needed. Resources are provisioned with more capacity than required. EBS volumes, snapshots, or networking resources are left unused and forgotten. Budgets are not monitored regularly, and increased spending is only discovered when the bill is reviewed. Cost Control focuses on monitoring spending, setting alerts, and controlling actions on resources. Cost Optimization has a broader scope, including adjusting resource configurations, removing idle resources, and choosing appropriate usage models.
Budget Controls for AWS acts as a budget control layer that helps send alerts and automatically manage certain resources when spending reaches predefined thresholds. It is not a complete cost optimization solution and should be combined with other resource management practices.
1.2. AWS Services Used Budget Controls for AWS uses several services to monitor budgets, evaluate resource tags, and perform automated actions.
Service Role AWS Budgets Tracks budgets and sends alerts when spending reaches configured thresholds. AWS Config Records configuration changes and evaluates resource tags. Amazon EventBridge Receives events and triggers processing steps. AWS Lambda Evaluates resources, adds tags, and processes notifications. Amazon DynamoDB Stores resource information and action history. Amazon SNS Sends alert emails and reports. AWS Step Functions Orchestrates the workflow that performs resource actions. AWS KMS Manages encryption keys for SNS topics. AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store Stores configuration parameters used by the workflow. AWS CloudFormation Deploys the solution’s resources. DynamoDB is created automatically by CloudFormation to store resource information and processing results. Amazon RDS Aurora is a resource type that the solution supports managing; it is not a database that must be created during deployment.
1.3. Overall Architecture AWS Budgets is responsible for monitoring spending, while AWS Config evaluates tags on supported resources. EventBridge, Lambda, DynamoDB, SNS, and Step Functions work together to record resources, perform actions, and send results.
Architecture diagram:
Figure 1. Overall architecture of Budget Controls for AWS.
The solution has two main workflows:
Tag management workflow: AWS Config evaluates resource tags. If a resource does not have a valid tag, EventBridge triggers the Lambda Remediation function to add the default value Inform. The information is stored in DynamoDB, and a notification can also be sent through SNS. Budget control workflow: AWS Budgets sends notifications to SNS when spending reaches a configured threshold. At the action threshold, Lambda triggers Step Functions. The workflow retrieves resource information from DynamoDB, determines the action based on the tag, and records the processing result. 2. BUDGET CONTROL AND RESOURCE MANAGEMENT MECHANISMS 2.1. Budget Monitoring with the 80% and 90% Thresholds In the default configuration described in the AWS article, the solution uses a monthly cost budget with two main thresholds:
When spending reaches 80% of the budget:
AWS Budgets sends a notification to the SNS Alert Topic. SNS sends an alert email to the registered address. At this threshold, the system only sends a notification; it does not stop or delete resources.
When spending reaches 90% of the budget:
AWS Budgets sends a notification to the SNS Action Topic. Lambda receives the notification and triggers AWS Step Functions to start the resource processing workflow based on tags.
The 80% and 90% thresholds are the solution’s default settings. Users can adjust the action threshold from 90% to 100%, following AWS guidance.
Note: AWS Budgets does not update cost data in real time. According to AWS documentation, data is refreshed up to three times per day, typically 8–12 hours apart. As a result, actual spending may already have exceeded a threshold before the notification is delivered.
2.2. Classifying Actions with the BudgetControlAction Tag The BudgetControlAction tag determines how a resource should be handled when the budget control workflow is triggered.
Tag value Meaning Action Inform Notification only Records the resource and sends information to the administrator. Stop Stop the resource Stops the resource if the service supports this action. Terminate Delete the resource Performs the deletion action according to the handling logic for each service. Inform is the default value. When AWS Config detects that a supported resource does not have the tag or has an invalid value, the resource may be evaluated as NON_COMPLIANT. Lambda Remediation is then triggered to add the default Inform tag.
Tag values are case-sensitive, so the exact values Inform, Stop, and Terminate must be used.
Several considerations apply when choosing an action:
For EC2, Stop stops the instance, but any retained EBS volumes may continue to incur storage charges. With Terminate, the EC2 instance is deleted. Whether its EBS volumes are also deleted depends on the DeleteOnTermination setting. For Amazon OpenSearch Service clusters, the workflow does not support the Stop action. The Inform and Stop values only send notifications; Terminate performs the deletion action. Therefore, Stop is suitable for test resources that can be restarted, while Terminate should only be used for resources that can be recreated and no longer contain data that must be retained.
2.3. Automated Workflow When the Budget Reaches the Action Threshold When spending reaches the 90% threshold, the workflow asks AWS Config to reevaluate supported resources to update their compliance status and tags.
Next, Step Functions retrieves resource information from DynamoDB, determines the action based on BudgetControlAction, and performs the required operation. The result is stored in DynamoDB for history tracking.
After Step Functions completes successfully, EventBridge triggers the Reporting Lambda to aggregate the results and send a report through SNS.
This workflow reduces manual management tasks. However, actions only apply to supported resources that are within the Stack’s management scope.
3. APPLYING THE SOLUTION AS PART OF AN AWS COST OPTIMIZATION STRATEGY Budget Controls for AWS helps control resources when spending reaches a threshold. To optimize costs more effectively, users should combine the solution with the following practices.
3.1. Monitor and Analyze Spending A suitable budget should be defined according to the purpose of the environment, such as learning, testing, or development. The 80% threshold provides an early warning so that administrators can review spending before the workflow reaches its action threshold.
In addition, AWS Cost Explorer can be used to analyze costs by service and time period, helping identify which components contribute most to the bill.
3.2. Classify Resources and Choose Appropriate Actions Administrators should select the BudgetControlAction tag according to the environment and the importance of each resource:
Development resources that need to remain available can be assigned Inform. Short-lived test EC2 instances that can be restarted can be considered for Stop. Temporary resources that can be recreated and do not contain data that must be retained can be considered for Terminate. The Terminate action should not be applied indiscriminately because it may cause data loss or application disruption.
In addition to the action-control tag, users should apply classification tags for project, environment, and owner to support cost tracking and allocation. BudgetControlAction does not replace tags used for cost management.
3.3. Right-Sizing and Managing Idle Resources Right-sizing is the process of adjusting resource configurations to match actual usage requirements and avoiding the allocation of more capacity than necessary.
For EC2, users can monitor CPU, memory, and network metrics to evaluate which instance type is appropriate. AWS Cost Explorer provides Rightsizing Recommendations to identify certain EC2 instances that may be over-provisioned. AWS Compute Optimizer also provides configuration recommendations based on utilization data.
For development and testing environments, users can schedule resources to start and stop according to working hours when the workload allows it. For workloads with changing demand, Auto Scaling can adjust capacity based on load.
Savings Plans or Reserved Instances may also be considered for stable workloads. Spot Instances are more suitable for tasks that can tolerate interruptions. These are additional Cost Optimization practices, not automatic features of Budget Controls for AWS.
3.4. Control Storage and Networking Costs Budget Controls for AWS does not manage every AWS resource. Therefore, components outside its supported scope may continue to incur costs even after an EC2 instance is stopped or deleted.
Users should review EBS volumes, snapshots, S3 buckets, NAT Gateways, and Elastic IP addresses. For infrequently accessed data, suitable S3 Lifecycle policies and storage classes can be considered. Volumes or snapshots that are no longer needed should also be reviewed and removed.
Stopping an EC2 instance does not mean that all related costs have been eliminated.
3.5. Evaluate Suitability for Real-World Environments Budget Controls for AWS is suitable for environments with many test resources that need a mechanism to control them when spending reaches a threshold.
In a learning environment, EC2 instances can be tagged with Stop if they can be restarted when needed. For a system serving users, Inform may be more appropriate so that the operations team can review the situation before taking action and avoid service interruptions.
Another limitation is that the solution does not manage all AWS resources. Even when an EC2 instance is stopped, related EBS volumes, snapshots, or networking components may continue to incur costs.
Therefore, Budget Controls for AWS should be considered a tool that helps enforce resource control policies. The effectiveness of Cost Optimization still depends on selecting appropriate actions, adjusting configurations, and regularly monitoring resource utilization.
4. HANDS-ON DEPLOYMENT AND TESTING WITH AMAZON EC2 The hands-on exercise was performed in the Asia Pacific (Singapore) – ap-southeast-1 Region, using EC2 as the test resource. DynamoDB, Lambda, EventBridge, and Step Functions were deployed through a CloudFormation template; their roles were analyzed based on the architecture and source code. Aurora was not created during the exercise.
4.1. Enable AWS Config Open AWS Config in the Singapore Region and use 1-click setup to configure resource configuration recording.
After setup is complete, check the status of the Config Recorder and Delivery Channel before deploying the CloudFormation stack.
Figure 2. Set up AWS Config and verify its operating status in the Singapore Region.
4.2. Deploy the Solution Using AWS CloudFormation Download the Budget Controls for AWS repository from AWS Labs and use the budgetcontrol_resources.yaml file.
Open the CloudFormation Console, select Create stack → With new resources (standard), upload the template, and provide the required information:
Stack name: BudgetControl. BudgetAmount: the monthly budget amount in USD. Notification email: the email address that must confirm the SNS subscription. The email parameter name must match the version of the YAML file being used. In the referenced template, the parameter is NotificationEmail; the repository README may display a different name.
Next, review the requested IAM permissions, create the Stack, and wait for its status to become CREATE_COMPLETE. Then open the email and confirm the SNS subscription.
Figure 3. Deploy Budget Controls for AWS using CloudFormation in the Singapore Region.
4.3. Create EC2 Instances and Check the Default Tag Create two EC2 instances in the same Region as the CloudFormation Stack:
bc-test-1. bc-test-2. After AWS Config records the configuration changes, the Custom Config Rule evaluates the BudgetControlAction tag on supported resources. If the tag does not exist or its value is invalid, Lambda Remediation may add the default value Inform.
Users can check the tag in the EC2 Console or AWS Resource Groups Tag Editor. Allow time for AWS Config to record and evaluate the resource before concluding that remediation has failed.
Figure 4. Check the BudgetControlAction tag on EC2.
4.4. Change the Tag Using the EC2 Console or Tag Editor Users can update the tag in either of the following ways:
EC2 Console: Select an instance, open the Tags tab, choose Manage tags, and edit the BudgetControlAction value. AWS Resource Groups Tag Editor: Select the Region, search for the tag, and update the selected resources. Example:
EC2 instance Tag value bc-test-1 Inform bc-test-2 Stop After updating the tag, check its value again to ensure that the change has been applied.
Note: Changing the tag to Stop does not stop the EC2 instance immediately. The tag only determines the action to be taken when the budget control workflow is triggered. Verifying that the Stop tag is present does not mean that the entire resource-stopping workflow has been successfully tested at the budget threshold.
Figure 5. Manage tags using AWS Resource Groups Tag Editor.
5. COSTS AND LIMITATIONS TO CONSIDER 5.1. Solution Operating Costs Budget Controls for AWS itself uses services that may incur charges, including AWS Config, AWS KMS, Lambda, Step Functions, DynamoDB, SNS, and CloudWatch Logs.
AWS Config can contribute significantly to variable costs because of Configuration Items recorded and Config Rule evaluations. Actual costs depend on the Region, the number of resources, and how frequently their configurations change.
5.2. Scope and Limitations Several important limitations should be considered:
One AWS account: Each Stack manages only one account. One AWS Region: The solution operates in the Region where the Stack is deployed. Limited resource types: The AWS article states that the solution supports EC2, RDS Aurora, SageMaker Notebook Instances and Domains, and OpenSearch clusters. It does not manage every AWS service. Resources outside the scope: Storage, networking, and unsupported services may continue to incur costs. Service-dependent actions: Not every resource type supports all three actions: Inform, Stop, and Terminate. Budget data latency: AWS Budgets does not update cost data in real time, so spending may continue to increase after a notification is sent. 5.3. Triggering and Cleanup Limitations According to the original AWS article, after the workflow performs an action, a resource may be restarted or recreated. However, the default workflow is triggered at most once per month unless the budget is adjusted to a higher level. When the budget moves into the next month, resources that were stopped or deleted are not automatically restored.
After completing the exercise, delete the CloudFormation Stack if it is no longer needed and check for remaining resources:
The BudgetControlAction tag may remain on resources. CloudWatch Log Groups and Aurora final snapshots may need to be checked separately. EC2 instances, EBS volumes, snapshots, and Elastic IP addresses should be reviewed to avoid continued charges. The AWS Config Recorder, Delivery Channel, and S3 bucket should be checked before deletion because other services may still be using them. After cleanup, check AWS Billing and Cost Management to monitor any remaining charges.
6. CONCLUSION Budget Controls for AWS is a solution that helps control costs by combining AWS Budgets, AWS Config, and automation services. Through its two default budget thresholds of 80% and 90%, users can receive alerts and trigger workflows to manage supported resources.
The BudgetControlAction tag allows users to select the Inform, Stop, or Terminate action. AWS Config evaluates the tag, Lambda helps add the default tag, DynamoDB stores resource information and action history, and Step Functions orchestrates the automated workflow.
The hands-on exercise with Amazon EC2 demonstrates how the solution can reduce manual management tasks and help limit costs from resources that are no longer needed. However, the solution does not manage every AWS service, budget updates are delayed, and the solution itself also incurs operating costs.
Therefore, Budget Controls for AWS should be viewed as one layer of protection within a broader Cost Optimization strategy, rather than a complete cost optimization solution. Sustainable cost management requires combining budget monitoring with right-sizing, idle resource management, and storage and networking cost controls.

IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary 2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? The Solution Benefits and Return on Investment 3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Use AWS CDK/SDK to code interactions (e.g., IoT Core rules to S3). Next.js reduces Lambda workload for the fullstack web app. 5. Timeline & Milestones Project Timeline
Pre-Internship (Month 0): 1 month for planning and old station review. Internship (Months 1-3): 3 months. Month 1: Study AWS and upgrade hardware. Month 2: Design and adjust architecture. Month 3: Implement, test, and launch. Post-Launch: Up to 1 year for research. 6. Budget Estimation You can find the budget estimation on the AWS Pricing Calculator.
Or you can download the Budget Estimation File.
Infrastructure Costs AWS Services: AWS Lambda: $0.00/month (1,000 requests, 512 MB storage). S3 Standard: $0.15/month (6 GB, 2,100 requests, 1 GB scanned). Data Transfer: $0.02/month (1 GB inbound, 1 GB outbound). AWS Amplify: $0.35/month (256 MB, 500 ms requests). Amazon API Gateway: $0.01/month (2,000 requests). AWS Glue ETL Jobs: $0.02/month (2 DPUs). AWS Glue Crawlers: $0.07/month (1 crawler). MQTT (IoT Core): $0.08/month (5 devices, 45,000 messages). Total: $0.7/month, $8.40/12 months
Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. Expected Outcomes Technical Improvements: Real-time data and analytics replace manual processes.
Scalable to 10-15 stations.
Long-term Value 1-year data foundation for AI research.
Reusable for future projects.

Week 3 Objectives: Understand the overview of Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) and its role in building and managing isolated virtual network environments on AWS. Understand basic networking concepts, including IP addresses, CIDR, Availability Zones, and how to divide a network into Subnets to organize AWS resources. Learn about the functions and operations of VPC networking components, including Subnets, Route Tables, Internet Gateway (IGW), and NAT Gateway. Understand network security mechanisms in VPC through Security Groups and Network Access Control Lists (Network ACLs), and distinguish their scopes and operating mechanisms. Gain practical knowledge and experience in creating VPCs, configuring Subnets, Internet Gateways, Route Tables, Security Groups, and VPC Flow Logs. Learn how to deploy Amazon EC2 Instances in Public and Private Subnets, establish SSH connections, configure NAT Gateways, and verify network connectivity. Become familiar with AWS network analysis and monitoring tools, including VPC Resource Map, VPC Reachability Analyzer, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, and Amazon CloudWatch. Understand AWS Site-to-Site VPN and the principles of establishing secure network connectivity between an On-premises environment and Amazon VPC through encrypted VPN tunnels. Gain practical experience in configuring Virtual Private Gateway (VGW), Customer Gateway (CGW), VPN Connection, and Libreswan software to establish Site-to-Site VPN connectivity. Understand the procedures for monitoring VPN Tunnels, customizing connection parameters, troubleshooting connectivity issues, and cleaning up AWS resources to minimize unexpected costs. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material 2 - Study the overview of Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) and its role in creating isolated virtual network environments on AWS.
- Learn about VPC network architecture and its basic concepts:
+ VPC: An isolated virtual network in AWS that allows users to control network configurations and deploy resources.
+ CIDR: The range of IP addresses allocated to a VPC and its Subnets.
+ Availability Zone (AZ): An independent location within an AWS Region that supports high availability for deployed resources.
- Learn about different types of Subnets:
+ Public Subnet: A Subnet with a route to the Internet through an Internet Gateway.
+ Private Subnet: A Subnet without a direct route to an Internet Gateway.
+ VPN-only Subnet: A Subnet configured with routes to a Virtual Private Gateway for VPN connectivity.
- Study Route Tables and their routing components:
+ Destination: The destination IP address or network range of traffic.
+ Target: The gateway or network component to which traffic is forwarded.
- Learn about Internet Gateway (IGW), its function in connecting a VPC to the Internet, and how to configure IGW routes in a Route Table.
- Understand NAT Gateway and how it allows resources in Private Subnets to initiate outbound Internet connections without allowing the Internet to initiate direct connections to those resources.
- Distinguish between NAT Gateway and NAT Instance.
- Study Multi-AZ network architecture and the benefits of distributing resources across multiple Availability Zones to improve availability. 19/10/2026 19/10/2026 Amazon VPC and AWS Site-to-Site VPN Workshop 3 - Study network security mechanisms in Amazon VPC:
+ Security Group: A virtual firewall that controls inbound and outbound traffic at the Network Interface or associated resource level.
+ Network ACL (NACL): A network traffic control mechanism applied at the Subnet level.
- Understand the differences between Security Groups and Network ACLs in terms of scope and operating mechanisms:
+ Security Groups are Stateful, meaning response traffic for permitted connections is automatically allowed.
+ Network ACLs are Stateless, requiring rules for both inbound and outbound traffic.
- Learn about Inbound Rules and Outbound Rules, including how to specify protocols, Port Ranges, and Source/Destination addresses when configuring security rules.

+ Verify connectivity between EC2 Instances and other components within the VPC.
+ Test Internet connectivity for resources configured in Public Subnets.
- Practice: Create and configure a NAT Gateway.
+ Allocate an Elastic IP Address for the NAT Gateway.
+ Create a Public NAT Gateway in the appropriate Public Subnet.
+ Associate the NAT Gateway with the allocated Elastic IP Address.

- Learn about CloudWatch Monitoring & Alerting and how to monitor EC2, NAT Gateway, VPN Connection, and VPC Flow Logs metrics.
- Understand how to configure CloudWatch alarms to monitor resources and detect network connectivity issues. 21/10/2026 21/10/2026 Amazon VPC and AWS Site-to-Site VPN Workshop 5 - Study the overview of AWS Site-to-Site VPN and its purpose in establishing secure network connectivity between an On-premises environment and Amazon VPC.
- Learn about Site-to-Site VPN architecture and the functions of its main components:
+ Virtual Private Gateway (VGW): The AWS-side VPN gateway attached to a VPC.
+ Customer Gateway (CGW): Represents the VPN device or software on the customer network side.
+ VPN Connection: The VPN connection established between a Virtual Private Gateway and a Customer Gateway.
+ VPN Tunnel: An encrypted communication tunnel used to securely transfer data between two network environments.
- Practice: Build a simulated Branch Office environment for VPN connectivity.

- Verify that all resources have been properly cleaned up to minimize unexpected AWS charges. 23/10/2026 23/10/2026 Amazon VPC and AWS Site-to-Site VPN Workshop Week 3 Achievements: Gained an overall understanding of Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) and its role in building isolated virtual network environments and managing AWS resources through user-defined network configurations.
Understood basic networking architecture and IP addressing concepts in VPC, including:
VPC: A logically isolated virtual network environment within AWS. CIDR: An IP address range used to define the network address space of a VPC and its Subnets. Availability Zone (AZ): An independent location within an AWS Region that supports resource distribution and high availability. Subnet: A subdivision of a VPC into smaller networks to organize and manage AWS resources. Distinguished different types of Subnets based on routing configurations and their purposes:
Public Subnet: Has a route to the Internet through an Internet Gateway. Private Subnet: Does not have a direct route to an Internet Gateway but can use a NAT Gateway to initiate outbound Internet connections. VPN-only Subnet: Configured with routes to a Virtual Private Gateway to communicate through a VPN connection. Understood the functions and operations of VPC routing components:
Route Table: Contains routing rules that determine how network traffic is forwarded based on Destination and Target. Internet Gateway (IGW): Allows resources in a VPC to communicate with the Internet when configured with public IP addresses and appropriate routes. NAT Gateway: Allows resources in Private Subnets to initiate outbound connections to the Internet or external services without allowing the Internet to initiate direct connections to those resources. Understood the differences between NAT Gateway and NAT Instance, as well as the role of NAT Gateway in allowing resources in Private Subnets to access the Internet through outbound connections.
Understood Multi-AZ architecture and the benefits of deploying resources across multiple Availability Zones to improve availability and reduce the risk of service disruption when an AZ experiences a failure.
Understood network security mechanisms in Amazon VPC, including:
Security Group: A virtual firewall that controls inbound and outbound traffic at the Network Interface or associated resource level and operates using a Stateful mechanism. Network ACL (NACL): A network traffic control mechanism applied at the Subnet level that operates using a Stateless mechanism. Inbound Rules: Rules that control incoming traffic to resources. Outbound Rules: Rules that control outgoing traffic from resources. Distinguished Security Groups and Network ACLs in terms of their application scope, operating mechanisms, and security rule configurations, while understanding the importance of allowing only necessary connections.
Became familiar with VPC Resource Map and learned how to use it to visualize relationships between VPCs, Subnets, Route Tables, Internet Gateways, and other network components in AWS.
Understood the function of VPC Flow Logs in recording IP traffic information flowing to and from Network Interfaces, supporting security monitoring, traffic analysis, and network troubleshooting.
Gained practical knowledge and experience in building an Amazon VPC environment, including:
Creating a Custom VPC named ASG with the IPv4 CIDR block 10.10.0.0/16. Enabling Enable DNS Hostnames and Enable DNS Resolution. Creating Public and Private Subnets in selected Availability Zones. Creating an Internet Gateway and attaching it to the VPC. Creating Route Tables and configuring the default route 0.0.0.0/0 to the Internet Gateway for Public Subnets. Associating Subnets with appropriate Route Tables. Creating and configuring Security Groups with Inbound Rules and Outbound Rules. Learning how to configure Network ACLs to control traffic at the Subnet level. Enabling VPC Flow Logs to monitor network traffic. Gained practical knowledge and experience in deploying Amazon EC2 Instances, including:
Selecting appropriate Amazon Machine Images (AMIs) and Instance Types. Configuring Key Pairs, VPCs, Subnets, and Security Groups. Deploying EC2 Instances in Public and Private Subnets. Checking EC2 Instance operational status, public IP addresses, and private IP addresses. Establishing SSH connections to EC2 Instances through Visual Studio Code and the Remote - SSH extension. Verifying connectivity between resources within the VPC environment. Understood how to deploy a NAT Gateway in a Public Subnet, allocate and associate an Elastic IP Address, and configure the Private Subnet Route Table to allow EC2 Instances to access the Internet through outbound connections.
Became familiar with VPC Reachability Analyzer and learned how to use the tool to:
Analyze network paths between resources within a VPC. Verify network connectivity based on current configurations. Examine Security Group and Network ACL rules. Identify configuration components that may affect network connectivity. Learned about EC2 Instance Connect Endpoint as an additional method of connecting to EC2 Instances without relying entirely on public IP addresses.
Understood the function of AWS Systems Manager Session Manager in securely accessing and managing EC2 Instances through interactive sessions with auditing capabilities, without requiring SSH Keys or opening inbound SSH ports.
Understood the role of Amazon CloudWatch in monitoring resources and network traffic, including:
Monitoring NAT Gateway metrics. Monitoring VPN Tunnel status and data traffic. Monitoring EC2 Instance performance, CPU, and memory metrics when corresponding metrics are available. Monitoring VPC Flow Logs and security events. Learning how to configure alarms when metrics exceed specified thresholds. Gained an overall understanding of AWS Site-to-Site VPN and how to establish secure network connectivity between an On-premises environment and Amazon VPC through encrypted VPN Tunnels.
Understood the functions of the main components in Site-to-Site VPN architecture:
Virtual Private Gateway (VGW): The AWS-side VPN gateway attached to a VPC to establish VPN connectivity. Customer Gateway (CGW): Represents the VPN device or software on the customer network side. VPN Connection: Establishes connectivity between a Virtual Private Gateway and a Customer Gateway. VPN Tunnel: An encrypted tunnel used to securely transfer data between two network environments. Gained practical experience in building a simulated Branch Office environment for VPN connectivity, including:
Creating a separate VPC named ASG VPN with the IPv4 CIDR block 10.11.0.0/16. Creating a Public Subnet and configuring an Internet Gateway. Creating a Route Table and configuring the necessary network routes. Creating a Security Group for VPN, SSH, and network connectivity testing. Deploying an EC2 Instance in a Public Subnet to act as the Customer Gateway. Checking the public IP address of the EC2 Instance. Gained practical experience in creating and configuring AWS Site-to-Site VPN components, including:
Creating a Virtual Private Gateway and attaching it to the target VPC. Creating a Customer Gateway using the public IP address of the EC2 Customer Gateway. Configuring the BGP ASN according to the workshop instructions, using the default value of 65000 in the static routing scenario. Creating a VPN Connection between the Virtual Private Gateway and Customer Gateway. Selecting Static Routing and specifying the network range 10.11.0.0/16 of the simulated Customer Gateway environment. Checking the VPN Connection status and connection initialization process. Understood the process of downloading and using the VPN configuration file provided by AWS for the Customer Gateway, including:
Selecting Vendor and Platform as OpenSwan. Selecting Software OpenSwan 2.6.38+. Selecting IKEv1 according to the workshop instructions. Using the configuration file as the basis for establishing IPsec on the EC2 Customer Gateway. Gained practical knowledge of installing and configuring Libreswan on the EC2 Customer Gateway, including:
Installing Libreswan on a suitable Linux environment. Checking and configuring the /etc/ipsec.conf file. Enabling IP Forwarding and configuring the necessary network parameters. Configuring IPsec parameters based on the AWS-provided configuration file. Checking VPN Tunnel status and verifying data transmission between the two networks. Understood how to customize VPN Tunnel parameters, including DPD Timeout, IKE versions, encryption algorithms, integrity algorithms, and Diffie-Hellman Groups.
Became familiar with enabling VPN Tunnel Activity Logs and using Amazon CloudWatch Logs to monitor VPN Tunnel activities, connection events, and information required for troubleshooting.
Understood the procedures for checking and troubleshooting Site-to-Site VPN connectivity issues, including:
Checking VPN Tunnel operational status. Verifying Customer Gateway and VPN Connection configurations. Checking IKE/IPsec parameters and authentication processes. Verifying IP Forwarding and routing information between the two networks. Examining network configurations and system logs to identify the causes of connectivity interruptions. Explored alternative VPN configurations and the StrongSwan with Transit Gateway connectivity model as optional workshop extensions.
Understood Infrastructure as Code (IaC) and the benefits of managing and deploying AWS infrastructure through machine-readable definition files, including:
Reusing configurations to deploy consistent environments. Managing versions and tracking infrastructure changes. Automating deployment processes to reduce manual errors. Recreating or cleaning up environments systematically. Supporting standardized infrastructure and security configuration checks. Recognized the importance of cleaning up AWS resources after completing practical exercises, especially NAT Gateways, Elastic IP Addresses, EC2 Instances, and VPN Connections, as these resources may incur charges during usage.
Understood the resource cleanup sequence recommended by the workshop to avoid dependency-related errors:
Terminate EC2 Instances. Delete NAT Gateways. Release Elastic IP Addresses. Delete VPC Endpoints, if any. Delete VPN Connections. Detach and delete Virtual Private Gateways. Delete Customer Gateways. Delete VPCs last. Understood that properly reviewing and cleaning up AWS resources helps minimize unexpected charges while keeping the AWS account environment organized and manageable.
